name: Across the Schools
description: The drawable items from the schools currently in this library, pooled into one grammar so a reading can sample across several at once. This is a partial collection and always will be — there is no complete set of the ways people have organised feeling. Each item links back to the school it came from and keeps that school's own words; the pooling is for reach, not for flattening them into a single house taxonomy.

Qíng and the Seven Emotions — Classical Chinese Medicine
Darwin — The Expression of the Emotions

sections.Definition: Core affect is a continuously present, continuously varying background state describable along two dimensions: valence (how pleasant or unpleasant) and arousal (how activated or calm). On this account it is always present — there is no affect-free baseline state a person returns to between emotions — and it exists prior to, and independent of, any emotion category being applied to it.
sections.Not a category, a dimension: Core affect is deliberately given no emotion_key, because it isn't a category candidate the way "anger" or "joy" are elsewhere in this collection — it's the raw material a concept gets applied to, not itself a named emotion. Two people (or the same person at two different times) can be in a similar core-affect state — unpleasant, highly activated — and construct it as anger, anxiety, or excitement depending on the concept and context available to them.
sections.Research note: Core affect draws on circumplex models of affect (notably James A. Russell's 1980 circumplex model of affect), which Barrett's framework incorporates as the pre-conceptual layer beneath category construction.

sections.Definition: Interoception is the brain's ongoing sense of the body's internal state — heart rate, breathing, gut activity, inflammation, and more — which this framework treats as continuously monitored and predicted by the brain as part of regulating the body's resources (its "body budget," the allostatic process of anticipating and meeting the body's metabolic needs before they become a crisis). Core affect is understood, on this account, as a summary readout of that ongoing interoceptive prediction, not a separate signal layered on top of it.
sections.Not a category, an ingredient: Like core affect, interoception is not itself a named emotion and carries no emotion_key here — it's one of the inputs a concept is applied to when the brain constructs a specific emotional instance.
sections.Research note: The body-budget framing draws on predictive-processing accounts of brain function (the brain as constantly generating predictions about incoming sensory and interoceptive data, updating on prediction error) applied specifically to interoception — a research direction with substantial and growing support in computational neuroscience, though the field's broader predictive-processing framework remains an active area of ongoing empirical work rather than settled consensus.

sections.Definition: On this framework, "anger" does not name one fixed inner state with one fixed facial or physiological signature. It names a population of highly variable instances — different combinations of core affect, interoceptive state, situation, and concept — that a perceiver (or the person themselves) categorizes as anger because the concept "anger," learned through language and culture, fits well enough in that moment. Two instances categorized as anger by the same person in the same week can differ substantially in their facial expression, physiology, and felt quality.
sections.Directly reusing the word other schools: This item deliberately shares its emotion_key with the "anger" items in Plutchik's wheel, Aristotle's rhetorical pathē, Aquinas's ira, and the basic-emotion school in this collection — not to claim they are all talking about the same fixed thing, but so the cross-grammar linking this whole library uses can surface the disagreement directly: click through and compare what each school claims "anger" is.
sections.Research note: The central empirical support cited for population-level variability in anger's expression and physiology is the 2019 meta-analysis by Barrett, Adolphs, Marsella, Martinez, and Pollak (Psychological Science in the Public Interest), which reviewed the wider evidence base and found no reliable one-to-one facial or physiological signature for anger, or for discrete emotion categories generally — the same study cited in this collection's basic-emotion and Plutchik-wheel schools as the direct empirical challenge to their own premises.

sections.Definition: As with anger, "fear" on this account names a variable population of instances rather than one fixed inner state — the same core-affect and interoceptive raw material that gets categorized as fear in one moment might, with a different concept available or a different context, be categorized as excitement, anxiety, or anger in another.
sections.Directly reusing the word other schools: This item's emotion_key deliberately matches "fear" as used in Plutchik's wheel, the Stoic and Aquinas schools (timor is keyed separately in Latin precisely because it is a narrower technical category, but is closely related), Darwin's chapter, and the basic-emotion school — the point of the shared key is to make the disagreement between this substrate and those schools directly comparable, item to item.
sections.Research note: Barrett and colleagues' own experimental work (e.g. studies manipulating context and interoceptive framing) reports that the same ambiguous bodily arousal state can be categorized by participants as either fear or excitement depending on situational cues — cited as direct evidence for construction rather than fixed triggering.

sections.Definition: As with anger and fear, "sadness" on this account is a variable population of instances built from core affect, interoception, situation, and a learned concept — not a single essence with one physiological or facial fingerprint that shows up the same way every time.
sections.Directly reusing the word other schools: This item's emotion_key deliberately matches "sadness" as used in Plutchik's wheel, Darwin's grief chapter (keyed as "grief" there, a related but not identical concept), and the basic-emotion school — again, so the cross-link makes the live disagreement visible rather than papering over it.
sections.Research note: Cross-cultural and within-culture variability in sadness's reported facial and physiological presentation is among the evidence the 2019 Barrett-led meta-analysis reviewed; the finding was not that sadness never involves a downturned mouth or slowed movement, but that no single configuration reliably and specifically marks sadness across contexts and individuals.

sections.Interpretation: You are experiencing or ready to experience profound joy. This is the height of positive emotion - a state of rapture and bliss. Ecstasy arrives when deep needs are met completely. It cannot be sustained but can be savored.
sections.Reversed: Manic energy without grounding. Chasing highs. Fear of ordinary contentment. What would it mean to let simple joy be enough?
sections.Evolutionary Function: Signals peak reward. In ancestors, marked finding abundant resources or successful mating. Reinforces life-enhancing behaviors.

sections.Interpretation: Joy signals that something life-enhancing is present. Plutchik saw joy as the emotion of incorporation - taking in what nourishes us. This is your birthright as a living being. What is bringing you joy?
sections.Reversed: Joy suppressed or denied. Guilt about feeling good. Waiting for permission to be happy. Joy is not earned - it is recognized.
sections.Evolutionary Function: Promotes bonding and approach behaviors. Signals safety and resource acquisition. The emotion of incorporation.

sections.Interpretation: Serenity is joy without urgency. A quiet okayness with what is. This gentle state is sustainable where ecstasy is not. Serenity comes when we stop fighting life.
sections.Reversed: Complacency mistaken for peace. Avoiding intensity. Serenity is not numbness - check if you're feeling or just coping.
sections.Evolutionary Function: Signals sustained safety. Allows rest and recovery. The parasympathetic state of contentment.

sections.Interpretation: Admiration is trust at its height. You see excellence, goodness, or beauty in someone or something. This emotion opens us to learning and growth. Who or what do you admire?
sections.Reversed: Idealization that ignores reality. Putting others on pedestals. Admiration can become projection - are you seeing them or your own unlived qualities?
sections.Evolutionary Function: Identifies models for learning. Promotes social hierarchy and skill acquisition through observation.

sections.Interpretation: Trust is the foundation of all relationship. Plutchik linked it to cooperation and mutual aid - essential for social species. Trust says 'I can rely on you.' Where is trust present or needed?
sections.Reversed: Naive trust without discernment. Or trust withheld from fear of betrayal. Both extremes cost us. Trust is a skill, not just a feeling.
sections.Evolutionary Function: Enables cooperation and group living. The basis of social bonds and reciprocal altruism.

sections.Interpretation: Acceptance is trust without intensity. A willingness to receive what comes. This isn't resignation but a soft yes to reality. Acceptance creates space for change.
sections.Reversed: Passive acceptance of what should be challenged. Not all situations deserve acceptance. Discern between peace and permission.
sections.Evolutionary Function: Reduces conflict and conserves energy. Allows integration into groups and adaptation to circumstances.

sections.Interpretation: Terror is fear beyond coping. The threat feels total. This ancient response helped ancestors survive predators. If terror visits you, find safety first - then process. The body remembers.
sections.Reversed: Terror that has lost its object but not its grip. Trauma echoes. Chronic terror needs gentle, supported healing.
sections.Evolutionary Function: Triggers freeze or flight in life-threatening situations. Maximum alertness for survival.

sections.Interpretation: Fear protects. It signals danger and prepares us to respond. Plutchik saw fear across all species - it's ancient wisdom. Fear asks: what needs protection? Honor it, then assess the actual threat.
sections.Reversed: Fear running the show. Threat detection without resolution. Fear is information, not a life sentence. What would courage look like here?
sections.Evolutionary Function: The primary protection emotion. Triggers fight-flight-freeze. Essential for survival.

sections.Interpretation: Apprehension is fear's quiet voice. Something feels slightly off. This subtle signal is easy to override but worth heeding. Apprehension asks for attention, not alarm.
sections.Reversed: Chronic low-grade anxiety. Apprehension that never resolves. Sometimes we must act despite unease. Distinguish signal from noise.
sections.Evolutionary Function: Early warning system. Promotes caution and risk assessment before full threat activation.

sections.Interpretation: Amazement stops time. Reality has exceeded your model of it. This is the emotion of encountering the truly new. Let amazement reorganize you.
sections.Reversed: Addicted to novelty. Ordinary life feels flat without amazement. The extraordinary is found within the ordinary, if you look.
sections.Evolutionary Function: Signals significant environmental change requiring attention and cognitive update.

sections.Interpretation: Surprise signals that something unexpected has occurred. It's neutral - the content determines if we shift to joy or fear. Surprise is the brain updating its predictions. What surprised you?
sections.Reversed: Nothing surprises anymore - either through rigidity or exhaustion. Life has lost its capacity to catch you off guard. Invite the unexpected.
sections.Evolutionary Function: Interrupts current processing for urgent reorientation. The reset button for attention.

sections.Interpretation: Distraction is surprise's whisper. Something catches your attention briefly. This can be noise or signal. Distraction may be pointing toward something worth noticing.
sections.Reversed: Chronic distraction without focus. Attention scattered. Not all distractions deserve following. What truly warrants your attention?
sections.Evolutionary Function: Low-level alert for peripheral changes. Balances focus with environmental monitoring.

sections.Interpretation: Grief is love with nowhere to go. It honors what mattered. Plutchik saw sadness as the call for comfort and reconnection. Grief needs witnessing, not fixing.
sections.Reversed: Grief stuck or avoided. Unmetabolized loss. Grief that doesn't move becomes depression. What loss needs mourning?
sections.Evolutionary Function: Signals significant loss. Elicits caregiving from others. Promotes social bonding through shared sorrow.

sections.Interpretation: Sadness signals loss or absence. Something needed is missing. This emotion draws others toward us with compassion. Sadness is how we honor what matters. What do you miss?
sections.Reversed: Sadness denied or indulged. Neither helps. Sadness asks to be felt and then to move. Are you feeling it or fighting it?
sections.Evolutionary Function: The reintegration emotion. Signals need for comfort and triggers helping behavior in others.

sections.Interpretation: Pensiveness is sadness's soft form. A wistful awareness of impermanence. This gentle melancholy can deepen appreciation for what is. There is beauty in pensiveness.
sections.Reversed: Wallowing in low-grade sadness. Romanticizing melancholy. Pensiveness is a visitor, not a residence. What would lift you slightly?
sections.Evolutionary Function: Promotes reflection and learning from loss. Conserves energy during low-resource periods.

sections.Interpretation: Loathing is total rejection. Something feels fundamentally wrong or contaminating. This intense disgust protects boundaries but can also poison the one who feels it.
sections.Reversed: Self-loathing turned inward. Loathing that has become identity. No one deserves to live in loathing - including yourself.
sections.Evolutionary Function: Maximum rejection response. Protects against contamination, poison, and moral violations.

sections.Interpretation: Disgust pushes away what is harmful or contaminating. Plutchik saw it as rejection - the opposite of incorporation. Disgust protects, but examine what you're rejecting and why.
sections.Reversed: Disgust turned rigid or arbitrary. Rejecting too much. Disgust can become prejudice if unexamined. Is this protecting you or isolating you?
sections.Evolutionary Function: The rejection emotion. Originally for bad food, extended to moral and social violations.

sections.Interpretation: Boredom is quiet rejection. Something fails to engage you. This can signal misalignment - you're in the wrong place. Or it can be an invitation to bring your own meaning.
sections.Reversed: Chronic boredom as a way of life. Everything irritates. This may signal deeper unmet needs beneath the surface irritation.
sections.Evolutionary Function: Signals low-value environment. Motivates seeking new opportunities and resources.

sections.Interpretation: Rage is anger beyond containment. Something important has been violated. This raw power needs safe expression - rage turned inward or outward carelessly causes damage.
sections.Reversed: Rage that has become chronic or identity. Rage covering vulnerability. What wound lives beneath this rage?
sections.Evolutionary Function: Maximum mobilization for threat destruction. Signals serious boundary violation requiring immediate action.

sections.Interpretation: Anger signals that a boundary has been crossed or an injustice occurred. Plutchik linked it to destruction of obstacles. Anger is information about what matters. What boundary needs defending?
sections.Reversed: Anger suppressed or chronic. Neither serves. Anger needs expression and resolution. What request or boundary would address this?
sections.Evolutionary Function: The destruction emotion. Mobilizes energy to remove obstacles and defend resources.

sections.Interpretation: Annoyance is anger's whisper. Small frictions accumulate here. Pay attention before annoyance builds. What small adjustment would help?
sections.Reversed: Chronic annoyance as a way of life. Everything irritates. This may signal deeper unmet needs beneath the surface irritation.
sections.Evolutionary Function: Early-stage anger. Signals minor obstruction requiring attention before escalation.

sections.Interpretation: Vigilance is anticipation at peak intensity. Every sense strains toward what's coming. Useful in genuine threat, exhausting as a lifestyle. What are you watching for?
sections.Reversed: Hypervigilance without rest. The sentinel who never sleeps. This intensity cannot sustain. What would let you rest your guard?
sections.Evolutionary Function: Maximum environmental scanning. Essential during danger or opportunity-rich periods.

sections.Interpretation: Anticipation looks forward. Plutchik linked it to exploration and mapping what's ahead. This emotion prepares us for what's coming. What are you anticipating?
sections.Reversed: Living entirely in anticipation, never in presence. The future devours the now. Can you prepare while also being here?
sections.Evolutionary Function: The exploration emotion. Motivates planning, preparation, and forward thinking.

sections.Interpretation: Interest is anticipation's gentle form. Something draws your attention forward. Follow genuine interest - it's a compass toward meaning.
sections.Reversed: Nothing interests. Flat affect. Interest suppressed or exhausted. What once interested you? Can you rekindle it?
sections.Evolutionary Function: Low-energy exploration. Promotes learning and curiosity without high arousal cost.

sections.Definition: In the basic-emotion model, anger is triggered by an appraisal of obstruction, unfair treatment, or a goal being blocked, and is claimed to produce a specific coordinated affect programme: lowered and drawn-together brows, a hard stare, tightened lips, and a physiological shift preparing the body for confrontation.
sections.The claimed signature: FACS work associates anger primarily with Action Units 4 (brow lowerer), 5 (upper lid raiser), 7 (lid tightener), and 23 (lip tightener), used together as the claimed marker researchers look for when coding anger from video or photographs.
sections.Research note: Cross-cultural recognition studies (Ekman & Friesen, 1971, among the Fore of Papua New Guinea) reported anger among the emotions recognized above chance across cultures using forced-choice tasks — a methodology later criticized on grounds discussed in this item's root.

sections.Definition: Disgust is triggered by an appraisal of contamination or offensiveness — originally, on this model, food-rejection, later extended to moral and social violations — and is claimed to produce a nose-wrinkle, raised upper lip, and a characteristic gape or grimace.
sections.The claimed signature: FACS work associates disgust primarily with Action Units 9 (nose wrinkler) and 10 (upper lip raiser), sometimes with 16 (lower lip depressor) added for more intense expressions.
sections.Research note: Disgust is among the emotions basic-emotion researchers have argued extended from a literal, ingestion-linked origin (rejecting a specific taste or smell) to abstract moral disgust — a claimed developmental and evolutionary continuity (see Rozin, Haidt, & McCauley's work on disgust's domains) that is itself a live area of ongoing research rather than settled fact.

sections.Definition: Fear is triggered by an appraisal of threat or danger, and is claimed to produce widened eyes, raised and drawn-together eyebrows, a horizontally stretched mouth, and physiological preparation for rapid escape or freezing.
sections.The claimed signature: FACS work associates fear primarily with Action Units 1+2 (inner and outer brow raiser), 4 (brow lowerer, often present alongside the raise, producing a distinctive combined shape), 5 (upper lid raiser), and 20 (lip stretcher).
sections.Research note: Fear's claimed expression overlaps partially with surprise's (both raise the brows and widen the eyes), which is part of why some forced-choice recognition studies report more confusion between fear and surprise than between more visually distinct pairs — a finding basic-emotion researchers and their critics read differently (see the root item's evidence_note).

sections.Definition: Joy (often labeled "happiness" in the original research literature) is triggered by an appraisal of goal-attainment or a rewarding outcome, and is claimed to produce a smile — specifically, in its most genuine form, a "Duchenne smile" involving both the mouth-corner-raising muscle and the eye-orbit muscle together, distinguished from a merely social or posed smile that uses the mouth alone.
sections.The claimed signature: FACS work associates genuine joy with Action Units 6 (cheek raiser, involving the muscle around the eye) plus 12 (lip corner puller); a smile using AU12 without AU6 is treated in this literature as a weaker or non-felt marker.
sections.Research note: The Duchenne-smile distinction traces back to 19th-century researcher Guillaume Duchenne de Boulogne, whose electrical-stimulation photographs Darwin reproduced and discussed in 1872 (see the darwin-expression school in this collection) — Ekman's research programme formalized and named the distinction, but did not originate the underlying observation.

sections.Definition: Sadness is triggered by an appraisal of loss or a goal that cannot be recovered, and is claimed to produce drawn-together and raised inner eyebrows, a downturned mouth, and, in some formulations, reduced overall muscular tone or slumped posture.
sections.The claimed signature: FACS work associates sadness primarily with Action Units 1 (inner brow raiser), 4 (brow lowerer, combined with 1 to produce an oblique inner-brow shape close to Darwin's own 1872 description of the "grief muscle"), and 15 (lip corner depressor).
sections.Research note: The oblique-eyebrow shape basic-emotion researchers describe for sadness is close to the same muscular pattern Darwin described in 1872 as characteristic of grief (see darwin-expression), one of the clearer direct through-lines between the two schools' specific claims.

sections.Definition: Surprise is triggered by an unexpected event, and is claimed to produce raised eyebrows, widened eyes, and a dropped jaw — a brief, fast-onset expression that basic-emotion researchers treat as the shortest-duration of the set, typically lasting well under a second before resolving into whatever emotion the surprising event turns out to warrant.
sections.The claimed signature: FACS work associates surprise primarily with Action Units 1+2 (inner and outer brow raiser, without the brow-lowering 4 that would shift it toward fear), 5 (upper lid raiser), and 26 (jaw drop).
sections.Research note: Because surprise is valence-neutral on its own (an unexpected event can turn out good or bad), some researchers within the basic-emotion tradition itself have questioned whether it belongs on the same list as the other five, which are each tied to a specific valenced appraisal — a question raised inside the tradition, not only by outside critics.

sections.Definition: In NVC practice, frustration typically points toward an unmet need for effectiveness, autonomy, or competence — the sense that one's efforts aren't landing, or that a choice one wants to make is being blocked. NVC asks the practitioner to locate the need underneath the frustration rather than stopping at the feeling or, worse, at blame directed at whoever seems to be causing it.
sections.Not a verdict about someone else: NVC draws a sharp line between a genuine feeling word ("I feel frustrated") and a pseudo-feeling that smuggles in a claim about another person's behavior or character ("I feel ignored," "I feel dismissed") — the second kind names a story about someone else's action, not a state in the speaker, and NVC practice asks a person to trace it back to the actual feeling and need underneath.
sections.Practice: The NVC move is not to suppress frustration or to blame its apparent cause, but to ask: what need of mine is unmet right now, and what specific, doable request could address it?

sections.Definition: Loneliness typically points toward an unmet need for connection, companionship, or being seen — NVC treats the feeling as accurate information about a real gap, not as a flaw in the person feeling it.
sections.Not a verdict about someone else: As with frustration, NVC distinguishes loneliness (a feeling) from a pseudo-feeling like "I feel abandoned" or "I feel unloved," which build in a specific causal story about another person's action or intent rather than simply naming the felt state and its underlying need.
sections.Practice: NVC's four-step practice model — a concrete observation, the feeling it brings up, the need underneath, and a specific request — is one route from loneliness to a workable next step: naming the observation ("we haven't spent time together this week"), the feeling (lonely), the need (connection), and a request ("could we set aside an hour on Thursday?") rather than an accusation.

sections.Definition: Anxious, in NVC's framing, typically points toward an unmet need for safety, security, clarity, or predictability — the sense that something important is uncertain or at risk. As with the other unmet-need signals here, NVC treats the feeling itself as useful data rather than as a problem to be argued away.
sections.Not a verdict about someone else: NVC would flag "I feel threatened" or "I feel set up" as pseudo-feelings if they're standing in for anxious plus an unexamined story about someone's intent — the practice asks the speaker to separate the felt anxiety from any claim about why it's happening.
sections.Practice: Naming the specific unmet need (safety? clarity? predictability?) underneath a general sense of anxious usually points toward a more answerable request than the vaguer feeling does on its own — a request for information, a timeline, or a check-in, rather than a request to simply stop feeling anxious.

sections.Definition: Relief typically signals that a need for safety, ease, or resolution has just been met — a tension that was present has resolved. NVC treats naming relief, and the specific need behind it, as just as useful a practice as naming a harder feeling: it builds the same fluency in the same direction.
sections.Practice: NVC materials commonly ask practitioners to also notice and name met-need feelings deliberately, not only to diagnose problems — naming what need relief is pointing to (here, ease or safety) makes it easier to recognize and ask for the conditions that produce that state again.

sections.Definition: Joyful, in this framing, typically points toward needs like connection, play, meaning, or contribution being met — NVC treats it, like every feeling on this deck, as a signal rather than a self-sufficient endpoint, worth tracing back to the specific need it's responding to.
sections.Practice: Naming which need is behind a joyful moment (was it connection? contribution? play?) is itself a practiced skill in NVC training, intended to build the same feeling-to-need fluency that the harder, unmet-need feelings require, so it isn't only exercised under difficulty.

sections.Definition: In Rhetoric II.2, Aristotle defines anger (orgē) as a desire, accompanied by pain, for conspicuous revenge for a conspicuous and unjustified slight directed at oneself or someone close to one. It is not raw physiological arousal; it is an appraisal — a judgment that one has been wronged and belittled — paired with the expectation that retaliation will be pleasant.
sections.Rhetoric-bound, not clinical: Aristotle is not describing anger as a state to be diagnosed or managed. He is telling an orator which beliefs make an audience angry — being slighted by people who owe them respect — so a speech can provoke that anger against an opponent, or calm it (praotēs, the paired state) in a judge who has been roused against the speaker's own client.
sections.Research note: Aristotle treats anger as an object-directed judgment rather than a mood — a cognitive-appraisal reading of emotion that anticipates, without duplicating, both Stoic theory and modern appraisal theories such as Richard Lazarus's (1991).

sections.Definition: Rhetoric II.8 defines pity (eleos) as pain at an apparently destructive or painful event happening to someone who does not deserve it, which the observer might expect could happen to himself or someone close to him. Both conditions matter: the suffering must look undeserved, and the observer must see it as possible for themselves — Aristotle notes that people who feel invulnerable feel less pity.
sections.Rhetoric-bound, not clinical: Pity here is a lever, not a syndrome. Aristotle catalogues what makes a courtroom audience pity a defendant — visible, specific, nearby suffering, a person like the listener — because a speaker who understands the lever can pull it.
sections.Research note: Aristotle explicitly pairs eleos with nemesis (indignation at another's undeserved good fortune) as mirror-image judgments about desert, not as unrelated feelings — a structural pairing this skeleton does not yet include as its own item.

metadata.deck: Greek Pathē — Rhetoric and Stoic Ethics

sections.Definition: In the Stoic scheme reported by later sources (chiefly Diogenes Laërtius and Stobaeus), lypē is an irrational contraction of the soul at what is wrongly judged to be a present evil. It is one of the four canonical pathē — a mistaken value-judgment about the present, not a physiological given.
sections.Why the Stoics call it irrational: For the Stoics, only virtue and vice are genuinely good or bad; everything else — health, wealth, reputation, even bodily pain — is "indifferent." Lypē arises from judging one of those indifferents to be a real evil. Because the judgment is false, the Stoics hold there is no well-reasoned version of it — unlike the other three pathē, lypē has no eupatheia (rational good-feeling) counterpart in the sage.
sections.Research note: This is an ethical claim about which judgments are true, not a description of a bodily process — reading lypē as equivalent to the modern clinical category "depression," or flattening it to the modern English word "distress," overstates the overlap in both directions.

metadata.deck: Greek Pathē — Rhetoric and Stoic Ethics

sections.Definition: Phobos, in the Stoic scheme, is an irrational shrinking-away from an expected evil — the future-facing counterpart to lypē's present-facing contraction. Like the other three pathē it is a judgment: that some coming indifferent is a real evil worth fleeing.
sections.Its rational counterpart: Fear's eupatheia is eulabeia, usually translated "caution" — a well-reasoned aversion to a genuine evil (vice, a wrong action) rather than to an indifferent thing. A Stoic sage, on this account, still avoids stepping off a cliff; the claim concerns which judgment does the avoiding, not the removal of self-preservation.
sections.Research note: The eupatheiai are attributed only to the sage — an ideal the Stoics themselves treat as rarely, if ever, instantiated. This is a normative model of how judgment should work, not a description of how most people's fear does work.

metadata.deck: Greek Pathē — Rhetoric and Stoic Ethics

sections.Definition: Epithymia is an irrational reaching-toward a future indifferent, wrongly judged to be a real good — the desire-pole of the Stoic four, paired conceptually with hēdonē (pleasure) the way phobos is paired with lypē: future versus present, in each case built on a mistaken value-judgment.
sections.Its rational counterpart: Epithymia's eupatheia is boulēsis, "wish" or rational will — desire aimed only at what is genuinely worth wanting: wisdom, justice, courage, self-command. The Stoics did not hold that a sage desires nothing; they held that a sage desires correctly.
sections.Research note: Later Stoic sources subdivide epithymia into a long list of named species — anger itself is sometimes classed as a form of it, a desire for revenge. This item covers the genus, not its species.

metadata.deck: Greek Pathē — Rhetoric and Stoic Ethics

sections.Definition: Hēdonē is an irrational swelling of the soul at a present indifferent, wrongly judged to be a real good — the present-facing counterpart to epithymia's future reach, and structurally opposite to lypē.
sections.Its rational counterpart: Hēdonē's eupatheia is chara, "joy" — a well-founded elation at something genuinely good, namely virtuous action itself, rather than at an indifferent circumstance. The Stoics distinguish chara sharply from hēdonē: the same felt shape, resting on a different object and a different judgment.
sections.Research note: Later Stoics, especially the Roman Stoic Seneca, develop chara at length as a durable good feeling available regardless of external circumstance — an idea with obvious later influence on Christian and secular therapeutic traditions, none of which this item claims as Stoic in origin.

metadata.deck: Greek Pathē — Rhetoric and Stoic Ethics

sections.Definition: Descartes places wonder (admiration) first among the six and treats it as unique: a sudden surprise of the soul that causes it to attend to and consider objects that seem rare or extraordinary — before the soul has judged whether the object is good or bad for it. Wonder is purely cognitive orientation toward novelty; unlike the other five, Descartes says it has no bodily opposite and does not depend on whether the object benefits or harms us.
sections.Why it comes first: Because wonder precedes any judgment of good or evil, Descartes treats it as the passion that makes the other five possible — nothing can become an object of love, hatred, desire, joy, or sadness until it has first been noticed as significant. Excess wonder, in his account, produces astonishment (étonnement), which can freeze a person into inaction; its useful degree he calls generosity of curiosity, a disposition to keep learning.
sections.Research note: This is the clearest point of contrast with basic-emotion models built around universal facial expressions (see the ekman-basic school in this collection): Descartes's wonder is defined by its relationship to prior knowledge (is this new to me?), not by any claimed facial signature.

sections.Definition: Descartes defines love as an agitation of the soul caused by the animal spirits, which impels the soul to join itself willingly to objects that appear agreeable to it — a felt movement toward union with something judged good, whether that something is a person, an object, or an idea.
sections.Its degrees: Descartes distinguishes affection (for something judged inferior to oneself), friendship (for an equal), and devotion (for something judged superior — God, one's country, one's sovereign). He treats these as differences of the same primitive passion rather than as separate ones.
sections.Research note: Descartes explicitly pairs love with hatred as its bodily and functional opposite (both concern union versus separation from an object), which is why they are grouped together in this deck's second-level composite.

sections.Definition: Hatred, in Descartes's scheme, is the mirror of love: an agitation caused by the spirits that impels the soul to will itself separated from objects presented to it as harmful. Where love draws the soul toward union, hatred drives it toward distance and rejection.
sections.Its physiology: Descartes ties hatred's bodily signature to a supposed bitterness in the blood and a tightening around the heart, part of his broader (and now superseded) mechanistic account of how each passion moves the animal spirits differently through the body.
sections.Research note: Descartes's specific physiology — animal spirits, the pineal gland as the soul's seat — is not treated as a live scientific claim by this school; his primitive-passion taxonomy is read independently of the 17th-century mechanics used to explain it.

sections.Definition: Desire is an agitation of the soul, caused by the spirits, that disposes it to will for the future whatever it represents to itself as agreeable — the only one of the six primitive passions Descartes defines as inherently future-facing.
sections.Its scope: Descartes treats desire broadly: it covers wanting to obtain a good one does not yet have and wanting to avoid an evil one fears, and even the desire to preserve a good one already possesses (since preservation is itself a kind of future-directed willing). He does not give desire a named opposite among the six.
sections.Research note: Descartes's desire is closer to what later philosophy calls a conative or motivational state than to a discrete felt emotion — it is defined by what it moves the soul to will, not primarily by how it feels.

sections.Definition: Joy is an agreeable emotion of the soul, in which the enjoyment it possesses consists — the felt experience of having, right now, what one has judged to be good. Where desire looks forward and love reaches toward union, joy registers a good already present or already attained.
sections.Its relation to love: Descartes treats joy as frequently accompanying love (one is glad about what one loves) but keeps them conceptually distinct: love is the movement toward union, joy is the register of possession. One can, on his account, love something one does not yet possess, in which case joy is absent and desire dominates instead.
sections.Research note: Descartes pairs joy with sadness as its direct opposite — both concern a good or evil the soul takes to be already present, rather than merely possible.

sections.Definition: Sadness is a disagreeable languor in which the soul's discomfort consists, arising from an evil, or a lack, that the soul represents to itself as belonging to it now — the counterpart to joy's registration of a present good, this time registering a present evil or absence.
sections.Its relation to hatred: As joy relates to love, sadness relates to hatred: hatred is the movement of rejection toward a harmful object, sadness is the felt discomfort of the evil or lack already being present. Descartes treats prolonged, ungrounded sadness as physiologically corrosive, and recommends attending to genuine present goods as a corrective — an early version of what later therapeutic traditions would call reappraisal.
sections.Research note: Descartes's six close on an opposing pair (joy/sadness) that mirrors the earlier pair (love/hatred), leaving wonder and desire as the two primitives without a named opposite in his own scheme.

sections.Definition: Amor is the first concupiscible passion: a connaturality or fittingness the sensitive appetite feels toward an apprehended good, prior to any movement toward or away from it. Aquinas treats it as the root passion from which desire and joy both follow — one desires what one first loves, and rejoices in possessing what one loves.
sections.The arduousness axis: Amor is concupiscible, not irascible, because it responds to the good simply as good — a fitting object, full stop — without regard to whether attaining or keeping it is difficult. Compare spes (hope), an irascible passion below: hope requires the good to be not just apprehended but hard to reach. Love does not.
sections.Research note: Aquinas distinguishes amor (a passion of the sensitive appetite, shared with animals in an analogous form) from caritas (charity, a theological virtue involving the will and grace) — this item concerns only the passion, not the virtue.

sections.Definition: Tristitia is the concupiscible passion of pain at a present evil apprehended as such — the counterpart to gaudium (joy) at a present good. Aquinas distinguishes several species by cause: pity (sorrow at another's evil), envy (sorrow at another's good, treated by Aquinas as a species of sorrow gone wrong), and anxiety (sorrow that weighs down the mind so it cannot see a way out).
sections.The arduousness axis: Tristitia responds to a present evil simply as evil, without regard to whether escaping it is difficult — which is exactly what separates it from timor (fear, an irascible passion, below): fear concerns a future evil that is hard to avoid, while sorrow concerns an evil already here.
sections.Research note: Aquinas holds that tristitia, unlike some passions, can be reduced by four specific remedies he names explicitly: weeping, the sympathy of friends, contemplating truth, and sleep or a bath — a concrete, almost clinical list embedded in an otherwise abstract taxonomy.

sections.Definition: Spes is the irascible passion of the appetite's movement toward a future good that is both possible to attain and arduous — difficult enough that attaining it is not a foregone conclusion. If the good were easy and certain, Aquinas holds, the appetite would simply desire it (a concupiscible act); it becomes spes specifically because obtaining it requires effort or struggle against resistance.
sections.Why the key is transliterated, not \"hop: English "hope" is used loosely for almost any positive expectation, easy or hard. Aquinas's spes is defined by the arduousness condition — no difficulty, no spes, just ordinary desiderium (desire). Keying this item as plain "hope" would erase the one feature that makes it irascible rather than concupiscible in the first place, and would silently merge it with every other school's much broader use of the English word.
sections.Research note: Aquinas pairs spes with desperatio (despair): both concern the same future arduous good, differing only in whether the appetite judges it attainable (spes) or not (desperatio).

sections.Definition: Timor is the irascible passion of shrinking from a future evil that is arduous to avoid — an evil difficult enough to escape that the appetite registers real resistance, not simply distaste. Aquinas catalogues species of timor by their object: laziness (fear of the effort a task requires), shame (fear of disgrace), and others.
sections.Why the key is transliterated, not \"fea: As with spes, the arduousness condition is what makes timor a distinct technical category rather than the everyday English word. An evil that is easy to avoid produces no timor in Aquinas's scheme, only ordinary aversion (fuga, concupiscible). Using plain "fear" as the key would quietly fold that structural distinction back into the very undifferentiated folk category this taxonomy exists to divide.
sections.Research note: Timor's irascible partner is audacia (daring), the passion of confronting rather than fleeing the same arduous evil — not included as its own item in this skeleton.

sections.Definition: Ira is the irascible passion of rising up against a present, arduous evil already inflicted — specifically, the desire to overcome or take revenge upon whoever caused it. Aquinas holds ira alone among the eleven has no contrary passion: there is no separate irascible passion of, say, meek acceptance of a present injury, because the irascible appetite's whole function is to confront arduous evil, and confronting it just is ira.
sections.Why the key is transliterated: Aquinas's ira is narrower than everyday English "anger": it specifically requires a present injury already suffered and a movement toward retribution against its cause — closer to what a modern reader might call righteous or retaliatory anger than to any irritation whatsoever. Keeping the Latin key flags that narrower scope rather than importing the full breadth of the modern word.
sections.Research note: Because ira has no contrary, it sits oddly against the rest of Aquinas's paired structure — commentators have long noted this as a structural asymmetry in the eleven-passion scheme, not an oversight this deck is introducing.

sections.Definition: Śṛṅgāra is the rasa built from the sthāyibhāva rati (love, romantic attachment). Bharata treats it as arising when a performance's determinants — a beautiful setting, the presence of a beloved, appropriate ornament and gesture — combine with the audience's own capacity to relish that theme, tasted rather than merely witnessed.
sections.An event, not a character's inner state: Śṛṅgāra does not belong to the character on stage (who may be performing convincingly without personally feeling love in that moment) nor simply to the spectator (whose ordinary daily love for a spouse is not itself śṛṅgāra). It is what arises in the relish of a spectator competent to engage with a well-built performance of rati — a three-way relation among craft, convention, and a trained aesthetic response, not a two-way transfer of feeling from actor to viewer.
sections.Research note: Bharata and later theorists (notably Abhinavagupta) subdivide śṛṅgāra into sambhoga (union) and vipralambha (separation) — the rasa of love-in-fulfillment and love-in-longing are treated as two registers of the same rasa, not opposites.

sections.Definition: Hāsya is the rasa built from the sthāyibhāva hāsa (mirth). The Nāṭyaśāstra treats laughter itself as graded — Bharata catalogues distinct types of laughter by intensity and by whose laughter it is (a refined character's smile differs, dramaturgically, from a low or vulgar character's laugh), and hāsya as a rasa is the audience's relish of that graded comic display, not the display alone.
sections.An event, not a character's inner state: A performance can present hāsa (a character being visibly amused) without producing hāsya in the audience, if the comic timing or convention fails — the rasa is contingent on the craft succeeding, not automatic from the content being nominally funny.
sections.Research note: Bharata pairs hāsya with śṛṅgāra causally in his own account — he holds that hāsya is in fact produced from śṛṅgāra (comedy as a kind of derivative or parody of the romantic), one of several explicit derivation relationships among the eight that this skeleton does not fully trace.

sections.Definition: Karuṇa is the rasa built from the sthāyibhāva śoka (grief, sorrow) — typically arising in performance from separation from loved ones, loss, curse, exile, or the destruction of what is cherished. It is the rasa most often invoked for tragic and elegiac performance across the Sanskrit dramatic tradition.
sections.An event, not a character's inner state: Karuṇa is the audience's aesthetic relish of well-performed śoka, not the raw distress a spectator would feel witnessing an actual death or loss. Classical commentary is explicit that rasa involves a kind of distance or generalization (sādhāraṇīkaraṇa) — the specific, personal edge of real grief is transmuted into a shareable aesthetic theme, which is part of why watching a tragedy can be pleasurable in a way that witnessing real grief is not.
sections.Research note: Bhāmaha and later theorists debate at length whether karuṇa's pleasure is genuine aesthetic pleasure or a paradox requiring separate explanation — a live question inside the tradition itself, not settled by Bharata's original text.

sections.Definition: Raudra is the rasa built from the sthāyibhāva krodha (anger), typically arising from confrontation, insult, betrayal, or battle — associated in the Nāṭyaśāstra with demonic and heroic characters (rākṣasas, and warrior figures in conflict) and with red as its governing color and Rudra as its presiding deity.
sections.An event, not a character's inner state: A performer displaying krodha through prescribed gesture, voice, and stance produces raudra in a spectator capable of relishing that display as craft — the rasa is not the actor's own anger (a trained performer is not actually enraged mid-performance) nor a contagious transfer of rage to the audience, but the aesthetic appreciation of anger skillfully rendered.
sections.Research note: Bharata links several rasa-pairs by claimed derivation; raudra is traditionally paired with vīra (the heroic rasa, not yet its own item in this skeleton) as sharing an active, high-energy register, in contrast to karuṇa's passive one.

sections.Definition: Bhayānaka is the rasa built from the sthāyibhāva bhaya (fear), arising in performance from threatening sounds, sights of danger, or the depiction of terrifying beings and situations — a register the Nāṭyaśāstra pairs closely with bībhatsa (disgust) and raudra as its neighboring negative-register rasas.
sections.An event, not a character's inner state: As with the other rasas, bhayānaka names the audience's relish of a well-built fear-display, not the character's or the audience's own visceral terror — a distinction the tradition needs precisely because genuine terror is not, in itself, an aesthetic pleasure, while bhayānaka, tasted at the right remove, is treated as one.
sections.Research note: Bharata's account of bhayānaka's typical determinants (vibhāva) — the sight of frightful forms, the sound of screams, an empty or dark space — reads as a fairly literal stagecraft manual for producing dread, distinct from a psychological theory of what fear itself is.

sections.Definition: Śānta, built from the sthāyibhāva śama (tranquility, or in some formulations the disposition toward liberation), was argued for as a ninth rasa by the 10th–11th century Kashmiri philosopher-aesthetician Abhinavagupta, several centuries after Bharata's original eight. Abhinavagupta treats śānta as, in a sense, the ground state underlying the other eight — the settled awareness from which any of the eight active rasas can arise and to which they return.
sections.A contested addition, argued rather than: Not everyone in the tradition accepted śānta as a rasa. Objectors held that a rasa requires an actively displayed sthāyibhāva — visible in a character's speech, gesture, and situation — while śama is precisely the absence or cessation of active emotional display, making it structurally unlike the other eight. Abhinavagupta's defense (developed at length in his Abhinavabhāratī commentary) is itself part of what makes śānta worth including here: it is a live philosophical argument inside the tradition, not a settled ninth entry Bharata himself endorsed.
sections.Research note: Abhinavagupta's broader philosophical commitments (he was also a major theorist of Kashmir Shaivism) inform his case for śānta — he connects aesthetic relish (rasāsvāda) to a state structurally similar to, though not identical with, spiritual realization (brahmāsvāda-sadṛśa, "resembling the taste of the absolute"), a controversial and much-discussed claim in later Sanskrit aesthetics.

items.name: Xǐ (喜) — Joy, Governed by the Heart

sections.Definition: Xǐ is paired with the heart (xīn) in the classical five-viscera correspondence. In modest degree it is considered healthy — the heart's proper state is described as one of ease and open communication with the world — but the Huangdi Neijing holds that excessive or sudden joy can scatter and slow heart qì, producing symptoms the text describes in terms consistent with what modern readers might call palpitations, restlessness, or difficulty concentrating.
sections.Wider than the English word: Classifying xǐ simply as "happiness" undersells how the classical texts use it: it names a specific quality and direction of qì movement (an outward, expansive, scattering tendency) tied to a specific organ system, not a private felt mood in the modern psychological sense. The pathology is about qì dynamics, not about mood valence as such.
sections.Research note: The claim that a specific emotion in excess damages a specific organ is a theoretical framework internal to classical Chinese medicine, built on the Five Phases (wǔxíng) correspondence system (heart–fire, in this case) rather than on the anatomical or biochemical mechanisms modern cardiology would investigate.

metadata.deck: Qíng and the Seven Emotions — Classical Chinese Medicine

items.name: Nù (怒) — Anger, Governed by the Liver

sections.Definition: Nù is paired with the liver (gān), whose classical function is to ensure the smooth, unobstructed flow of qì throughout the body. Anger is held to cause qì to rise and rush upward and outward — the Neijing associates excessive nù with liver qì stagnation or liver-yang rising, described in symptom-language including headache, a flushed face, and irritability.
sections.Wider than the English word: As with xǐ, nù names a directional qì disturbance (an upward, forceful surge) associated with a specific organ system's proper function being disrupted, not a discrete inner feeling considered on its own. Frustration, resentment, and irritability are often discussed under the same liver-qì framework even where the English words would distinguish them.
sections.Research note: The liver–anger pairing is one of the most frequently cited five-viscera correspondences in both classical sources and contemporary Traditional Chinese Medicine clinical practice, though contemporary TCM's own systematization dates mainly to 20th-century standardization efforts building on, but not identical to, the classical texts.

metadata.deck: Qíng and the Seven Emotions — Classical Chinese Medicine

items.name: Sī (思) — Pensiveness/Overthinking, Governed by the Spleen

sections.Definition: Sī is paired with the spleen (pí), the organ classically responsible for transforming food into qì and blood. Sī names sustained mental concentration, worry, or rumination — Bharata's rasa school and this school share nothing structurally, but sī resembles neither pure "thought" nor pure "emotion" in the English sense: it sits at the seam between the two, which is exactly the kind of category the English word "emotion" does not have room for.
sections.Why this key is transliterated, not \"wo: English forces a choice between a cognitive gloss ("overthinking," "rumination") and an affective one ("worry," "anxiety"), and either choice discards half of what sī names in the source texts: a single qì-disturbing pattern of dwelling on something, cognitively and affectively at once. Picking one English word would silently resolve an ambiguity the classical texts do not resolve.
sections.Research note: The Neijing holds that excessive sī knots spleen qì, impairing its transforming function — described in symptom-language including poor appetite, fatigue, and a bloated or heavy sensation, consistent with the digestive role assigned to the spleen in this system.

metadata.deck: Qíng and the Seven Emotions — Classical Chinese Medicine

items.name: Bēi (悲) — Grief, Governed by the Lung

sections.Definition: Bēi is paired with the lung (fèi), classically responsible for governing qì and respiration. Grief and sorrow are held to disperse or deplete lung qì, and the Neijing associates prolonged bēi with shortness of breath, a sunken or withdrawn bearing, and general depletion of vital energy.
sections.Wider than the English word: Some classical sources pair the lung with yōu (worry, anxious brooding) rather than, or alongside, bēi (grief proper) — the seven-emotion list and the five-viscera list do not map onto each other item-for-item, and different texts group yōu and bēi together under the lung differently. This item follows the more common grief-lung pairing; the worry-lung variant is noted here rather than given its own entry.
sections.Research note: The lung's classical association with grief has an often-cited resonance with the Five Phases correspondence of metal (associated with autumn, decline, and letting go) to the lung — a symbolic-seasonal logic distinct from, and not reducible to, a modern respiratory-physiology account of sadness.

metadata.deck: Qíng and the Seven Emotions — Classical Chinese Medicine

items.name: Kǒng (恐) — Fear, Governed by the Kidney

sections.Definition: Kǒng is paired with the kidney (shèn), classically the organ storing jīng (essence) and considered the root of the body's constitutional reserves. Kǒng is held to cause qì to sink and descend, and prolonged fear is associated in the Neijing with depletion of kidney essence — described in symptom-language including weakness in the low back and knees, and in more severe classical descriptions, loss of bladder control under acute fright.
sections.Wider than the English word: The classical texts distinguish kǒng (a more settled, dwelling fear or apprehension) from jīng (a sudden fright or shock, sometimes counted as a separate seventh emotion, sometimes folded into kǒng depending on the source) — a distinction of duration and suddenness that plain English "fear" does not mark on its own.
sections.Research note: The kidney's role as the body's constitutional root makes fear's association with it medically significant within the system: kidney depletion is treated as a serious, slow-to-recover condition, so chronic kǒng is regarded as a comparatively grave pattern rather than a passing state.

metadata.deck: Qíng and the Seven Emotions — Classical Chinese Medicine

sections.Definition: Darwin describes grief's characteristic muscular signature in detail: the contraction of the corrugator muscle drawing the eyebrows together and slightly upward into an oblique shape he calls the "grief muscle," often accompanied by a downturned mouth and, in acute grief, weeping. He treats infant crying as the developmentally earliest form and argues the adult oblique-eyebrow pattern derives from the same underlying muscular action, tempered by the acquired habit of restraining full infant-style crying.
sections.The explanatory principle at work: Darwin attributes weeping partly to the direct action of the nervous system — violent, prolonged screaming in infants engorges blood vessels around the eyes, and reflex contraction of the surrounding muscles to protect them is, on his account, the origin of tear secretion during distress, later retained as an involuntary accompaniment to grief even without the original screaming.
sections.Research note: Darwin's chapter draws on his own observation of his infant children (recorded in a private notebook years before this book, later incorporated into it), an early and unusually longitudinal source of developmental data for its period.

metadata.deck: Darwin — The Expression of the Emotions

sections.Definition: Darwin describes fear's expression as widened eyes with visible white above the iris, raised eyebrows, a pale face (from blood withdrawing to the internal organs), trembling, erect hair (piloerection), and a general muscular readiness that can tip into either flight or immobility.
sections.The explanatory principle at work: Fear's trembling is Darwin's central example of the direct-action-of-the-nervous-system principle: he argues trembling serves no purpose in itself and is simply what happens when strong nervous excitement disrupts the ordinary, coordinated control of the muscles — a byproduct, not a signal. Piloerection, by contrast, he explains through continuity with other animals, where raised hair or feathers make a frightened or threatened animal look larger to a predator or rival.
sections.Research note: Darwin's cross-cultural questionnaire (circulated to missionaries and colonial officials) specifically asked whether fear's facial signs — widened eyes, pallor — were recognized as such among populations the respondents worked with, an early and methodologically crude precursor to the controlled cross-cultural studies Paul Ekman would run roughly a century later (see the ekman-basic school in this collection).

metadata.deck: Darwin — The Expression of the Emotions

sections.Definition: Darwin describes anger's expression as a flushed or reddened face, dilated nostrils, a firmly closed or square-shaped mouth, a direct and fixed stare, and — in its more intense forms — bared teeth and a lowered, forward head posture he treats as directly continuous with an animal's threat display before biting or charging.
sections.The explanatory principle at work: Anger's teeth-baring is Darwin's flagship example of a serviceable associated habit: teeth-baring once served the direct purpose of preparing to bite an opponent; humans retain the habit — an involuntary curl of the upper lip, a partial baring of the canine — as a vestigial residue of that ancestral function, even in contexts (a heated argument) where biting is not remotely in question.
sections.Research note: Darwin explicitly draws the comparison to snarling dogs and other animals baring teeth before attack, using it as one of his central pieces of evidence for continuity of expression across species rather than a special, separately-evolved human signal.

metadata.deck: Darwin — The Expression of the Emotions

sections.Definition: Darwin treats joy's principal expression as laughter and smiling: contraction of the muscles around the eyes and mouth (he specifically notes the involvement of the muscle that produces crow's-feet wrinkling around the eyes in a genuine smile — an observation later formalized as part of the Duchenne marker in 20th-century facial-expression research), combined with the characteristic rhythmic vocalization of laughter itself.
sections.The explanatory principle at work: Darwin applies antithesis here directly: he holds that joy's characteristically open, upward, expansive bodily posture is, in part, simply the physical opposite of grief and low spirits' contracted, downward posture — not because the open posture itself serves any function, but because a state of mind opposite to a purposeful one tends to produce movements that are its physical opposite.
sections.Research note: Darwin's observation about eye-muscle involvement in genuine versus posed smiling anticipates, without naming, what 20th-century researcher Guillaume Duchenne de Boulogne's electrical-stimulation photographs (which Darwin himself reproduced with permission in this book) and later facial-coding systems would formalize as the distinction between a "Duchenne smile" and a merely social one.

metadata.deck: Darwin — The Expression of the Emotions

sections.Definition: Darwin devotes his final substantive chapter to blushing, which he calls "the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions." He describes it as an involuntary reddening of the face, ears, and neck caused by dilation of the facial capillaries, typically triggered by the awareness — real or imagined — of being noticed and judged by others, rather than by shame or embarrassment in private with no observer present.
sections.Why Darwin treats it as uniquely human: Unlike anger's teeth-baring or fear's piloerection, Darwin argues blushing has no clear precursor in other animals and no obvious prior serviceable function of its own — he treats it as arising indirectly, through the attention a person pays to their own face when self-conscious, which he proposes causes local vasodilation there specifically rather than elsewhere on the body. He treats this as one of the harder cases for his own three-principle framework to explain cleanly, and says so.
sections.Research note: Darwin's own questionnaire respondents reported blushing (or its absence, or local variants like darkening rather than reddening in populations with more melanin) across a wide range of cultures he had access to via missionary and colonial networks — evidence Darwin read as supporting a universal, evolved mechanism rather than a culturally taught social display, though the questionnaire method itself (untrained observers, leading questions, no standardized recording) falls well short of later controlled cross-cultural methodology.

metadata.deck: Darwin — The Expression of the Emotions

sections.Definition: Aristotle's Rhetoric analyzes pathē as levers an orator can pull, not as a fixed inner inventory: a pathos is defined by the situation that provokes it, the state of the person it targets, and the grounds on which it can be talked up or down. The Nicomachean Ethics gives a broader, differently-membered list for a different purpose. There is no single canonical Aristotelian emotion list — the count and membership shift with the text's aim, which is itself the first data point in this genealogy.

items.name: The Stoic Classification of the Pathē

sections.Definition: The Stoics, beginning with Chrysippus's On Passions, rebuilt the apparatus around an entirely different question than Aristotle's: not what moves an audience, but what a mistaken judgment does to the soul. Four pathē genera (distress, fear, appetite, pleasure) sit against three eupatheiai, rational good feelings available to the wise. The organizing axis is epistemic — whether the underlying judgment is true or false, present or future — not valence and not a body-part inventory.

Aquinas's Summa Theologiae (Prima Secundae, Qq. 22–48) inherits Aristotle's pathē by way of the Latin passiones and reorganizes them around the soul's two sensitive appetites: six concupiscible passions in three pairs (love/hatred, desire/aversion, joy/sorrow), and five irascible passions (hope/despair, fear/daring, plus anger, which Aquinas holds has no contrary). The organizing axis is the arduousness of the object — difficult to attain or avoid — not pleasant-versus-unpleasant. Hope and fear sit together not because they feel alike but because both concern a hard-to-reach good or evil.

Descartes's Les passions de l'âme (1649) names six passions he calls primitive — wonder, love, hatred, desire, joy, sadness — as causal building blocks compounded by the mechanics of the pineal gland and animal spirits, not a claim about universal cross-cultural recognition.
sections.Research note: Worth stating precisely, since it is easy to conflate with a much later list: Descartes's six are not Ekman's six. Only love/joy and hatred/sadness are even loosely analogous; wonder and desire have no Ekman counterpart, and surprise, disgust, and fear have no Cartesian one. The idea of "six basic passions/emotions" has a European philosophical pedigree that predates Ekman by roughly three hundred years, with an entirely different membership and an entirely different theoretical basis.

sections.Definition: Spinoza's Ethics (published posthumously, 1677), written in explicit and often critical dialogue with Descartes, reduces the primitives further to three: desire, joy, and sadness — defined not as felt qualities but as transitions in the body's power of acting. Every other affect (love, hate, hope, fear, pride) is one of these three entangled with the idea of an external cause.

Hume's A Treatise of Human Nature (1739) splits the passions along a third seam entirely: direct passions (desire, aversion, grief, joy, hope, fear) arise immediately from pleasure or pain, while indirect passions (pride, humility, love, hatred) additionally require an idea of self or another person as their object. Neither Descartes's causal-primitive axis nor Spinoza's power-of-acting axis nor Aquinas's arduousness axis appears here — Hume's cut is about what the passion is about.
sections.Research note: Three major European thinkers, working within roughly ninety years of each other in the same broad conversation, produced three structurally incompatible taxonomies with three different primitive counts. This is the clearest pre-modern evidence that a "basic emotions" list is a design choice remade to fit an argument, not a discovery converged on from different angles.

sections.Definition: Thomas Dixon's From Passions to Emotions argues that "the emotions," as one English category spanning everything from a startle reflex to religious rapture, is a nineteenth-century invention rather than a discovery of something always there under older names. Earlier English vocabulary distinguished passions (strong, morally dangerous movements), affections (steadier, morally approved inclinations), and sentiments (refined, socially calibrated feelings, per Hume and Adam Smith). Scottish thinkers, especially Thomas Brown and Thomas Chalmers, began collapsing these; physicalist, increasingly secular writers after them — Alexander Bain, Herbert Spencer, and eventually Darwin — completed the consolidation.
sections.Research note: This is a gradual nineteenth-century process spanning several named thinkers, not a single dated event; the era label reflects that. If the container itself is a comparatively recent, English-language, secularizing artifact, universality claims about what fills that container are being asked to do work before the container's own boundaries have been justified — this is Dixon's argument, presented here as his, not as this deck's settled verdict.

sections.Definition: Darwin's The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals (1872) argues that facial and bodily expressions are largely innate and adaptive, evidenced by their appearance in infants, in people born blind, and across species none of whom could have learned them by imitation. Darwin supplemented direct observation and Duchenne de Boulogne's photographic studies with a network of questionnaires sent to missionaries and colonial travelers — an early, methodologically loose ancestor of the cross-cultural "universality" study design later formalized by Ekman, and one of the earliest documented contact points between this lineage and the others this deck follows.

metadata.when: 1872 (The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals)

sections.Definition: James's 1884 essay "What Is an Emotion?", extended in The Principles of Psychology (1890), proposes the opposite causal order from ordinary intuition: bodily changes come first, and the feeling of those changes is the emotion — strip away the bodily feedback and, James argued, nothing recognizable as the emotion is left. Independently proposed around the same time by the Danish physiologist Carl Lange, hence "James–Lange theory." James located emotion in specific, differentiated bodily patterns per emotion, where later constructionist accounts locate it in a much more general, undifferentiated signal categorized after the fact.

Silvan Tomkins's Affect Imagery Consciousness (1962–63) proposed nine innate affects — interest-excitement, enjoyment-joy, surprise-startle, fear-terror, distress-anguish, anger-rage, shame, disgust, and "dissmell" — as hard-wired subcortical programs, largely independent of drives like hunger and sex, arguing that affect rather than drive is the primary motivator of behavior. Tomkins mentored a generation of researchers, Paul Ekman among them, who took the hard-wired-universal-discrete-affect idea forward into cross-cultural facial-expression research.

items.name: Ekman's Six Basic Emotions and FACS

sections.Definition: Ekman narrowed Tomkins's nine down, in most published statements, to six — anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise — argued to be universal across cultures on the strength of fieldwork with the Fore of Papua New Guinea (published as "Constants Across Cultures in the Face and Emotion," 1971). With Wallace Friesen, Ekman built the Facial Action Coding System (FACS, 1978), an anatomically grounded notation for facial-muscle movement.
sections.Research note: The classic Fore studies used a forced-choice design — matching a face to one of a short supplied list of words or stories — which cannot, by construction, show that a culture independently carves feeling into those categories; it can only show that people can match faces to a supplied list better than chance. Later free-labelling and free-sorting studies, including Gendron and Barrett's Himba fieldwork, generally found weaker, more context-dependent agreement. This is a live, ongoing dispute rather than a settled question — see this deck's own constructed-emotion school for the counter-position.

metadata.when: 1971 (Ekman & Friesen, Constants Across Cultures in the Face and Emotion)

sections.Definition: Robert Plutchik, working independently within a psychoevolutionary framework rather than from facial-universality data, proposed eight primary emotions — joy, trust, fear, surprise, sadness, disgust, anger, anticipation — arranged in 1980 as a wheel of four opposing pairs, with intensity increasing toward the center and adjacency-blends ("dyads") at the outer edge.
sections.Research note: Plutchik's eight and Ekman's six overlap on most terms but are not the same list, and were built from different theoretical starting points published within a few years of each other. Even inside the mid-twentieth-century "basic emotions" consensus, there was no actual agreement on count or membership — only on the architecture of discrete, universal, biologically basic categories.

sections.Definition: James Russell's 1980 circumplex model discarded discrete categories in favor of two continuous, bipolar dimensions — pleasure/displeasure and arousal/sleepiness — onto which any feeling word can be plotted as a point rather than sorted into a bin. In a 1994 review, Russell directly challenged the evidentiary basis of the "universal recognition" literature, arguing the apparent universality was substantially an artifact of study design — a critique later extended by Barrett's group.

Lisa Feldman Barrett's theory of constructed emotion, synthesized in How Emotions Are Made (2017), proposes that emotion is not a triggered program but a real-time construction: the brain continuously generates a general, undifferentiated core-affect signal — a point in valence-arousal space, descended from Russell's circumplex — from interoceptive and exteroceptive input, then categorizes that signal in the moment using concepts learned from language and culture.

Bharata Muni's Nāṭyaśāstra sets out eight rasas — the erotic, comic, pathetic, furious, heroic, fearful, odious, and marvelous — each produced in an audience by the corresponding stable emotion (bhāva) of the character portrayed. A rasa is not, in the first instance, a state inside a person's body; it is what a well-made performance produces in a qualified spectator, an aesthetic "flavor" distilled from a character's felt emotion. The unit of analysis is the relationship between performer, text, and audience, not an individual's physiology.
sections.Research note: The Nāṭyaśāstra's own composition date is a live scholarly estimate, not a fixed point — sources place it anywhere across roughly four centuries. The era label here reflects that spread rather than a single agreed year.

metadata.era: roughly 200 BCE – 200 CE (scholarly estimate spans several centuries)

sections.Definition: Roughly a millennium after Bharata, the Kashmiri philosopher Abhinavagupta, commenting on the Nāṭyaśāstra in his Abhinavabhāratī, argued that Bharata's eight rasas were incomplete and added a ninth, śānta (peace, tranquility) — and, working within a nondual Śaiva framework, argued śānta is not merely one rasa among nine but the ground the other eight relish against.
sections.Research note: Whether śānta is best read as a ninth peer category or as a substrate-like ground for the other eight is a live question within rasa scholarship itself, not settled here — a structural echo, worth naming without overstating the parallel, of this library's own claim that constructed emotion is a frame rather than a peer school.

items.name: The Seven Emotions of Classical Chinese Medicine

sections.Definition: The Huangdi Neijing (Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic) and later texts organize feeling into the "seven emotions" (qīqíng) — joy, anger, worry, pensiveness, grief, fear, and fright — each in correspondence with one of the five viscera: the heart governs joy, the liver anger, the spleen contemplation, the lung grief, the kidney fear. The organizing axis is a physiological correspondence system, where an emotion in excess becomes a pathogenic factor — too much anger injures the liver, too much grief the lung — folding feeling directly into a theory of disease rather than a theory of mind.
sections.Research note: Chinese qing (情) is broader than the English "emotion," carrying senses closer to "circumstance" or "the facts of a matter" in classical usage — a claim drawn from general background on classical Chinese moral psychology rather than a single checked source, and flagged here as unverified rather than asserted as settled.

metadata.when: c. 2nd c. BCE – 3rd c. CE (Huangdi Neijing, Han dynasty compilation, 206 BCE – 220 CE)

sections.Definition: Synthesized across decades of Amazonianist ethnography by the Brazilian anthropologist Eduardo Viveiros de Castro, Amerindian perspectivism does not produce a taxonomy of feelings, and that absence is the finding, not a gap. Across a range of Amazonian cosmologies, what differs between kinds of being (human, jaguar, spirit) is not the emotional repertoire but the world each kind of body discloses — multinaturalism: one shared culture (the capacity to be a point of view) and many natures, in deliberate inversion of Western multiculturalism's one nature, many cultures.
sections.Research note: This document worked primarily from Viveiros de Castro's 2004 restatement ("Perspectival Anthropology and the Method of Controlled Equivocation," Tipití) and secondary overviews rather than the full text of the foundational 1998 article ("Cosmological Deixis and Amerindian Perspectivism," Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute) — a distance from the primary source worth naming rather than smoothing over.

metadata.when: 1998 (foundational statement; this deck also draws on the 2004 restatement)

items.name: Lutz's Ifaluk Fieldwork — fago and song

sections.Definition: Catherine Lutz's Unnatural Emotions: Everyday Sentiments on a Micronesian Atoll and Their Challenge to Western Theory (1988), based on fieldwork on Ifaluk atoll in 1977–78, documents an emotion vocabulary organized around relationship and moral order rather than a private interior state to be labeled. Fago is felt toward someone suffering, in need, or leaving, and binds compassion, love, and grief together in a way English does not; song is specifically justifiable anger, sanctioned within Ifaluk moral order in a way undifferentiated English "anger" is not.
sections.Research note: This is the most recent fieldwork of the five lineages this deck follows, and the only one built on direct, extended ethnographic immersion rather than a canonical philosophical or medical text — which also means the evidentiary basis for fago and song is a single ethnographer's fieldwork record, rich but not independently replicated by other fieldworkers to this document's knowledge. A gloss ("compassion," "anger") is accurate enough to pass a forced-choice check and wrong enough to lose the concept's actual shape — Lutz's own definitions are given here before, not instead of, the nearest English word.
